analysis.one_liner: Requires social media, gaming, and messaging platforms to build safety safeguards and parental controls for users under 17.
analysis.headline: A kids' online safety bill with 76 Senate cosponsors from both parties cleared the Senate Commerce Committee favorably on August 5, 2026, but has not yet received a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make online platforms, video games, and streaming services take reasonable care in designing features so they do not harm users under 17. It would require platforms to give minors strong safety settings by default, give parents tools to manage a child's account, ban ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol aimed at minors, and force big platforms to publish yearly independent audits of how minors use them. It would also let users turn off algorithms that rank content based on their personal data. Enforcement would run through the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers who use social media, video games, and messaging apps, along with their parents. Minors would get the most protective privacy and safety settings turned on by default, an easy way to opt out of algorithmic feeds, limits on who can contact them, and controls on their location data. Parents would be able to view and manage their child's settings, see how much time the child spends on the platform, and restrict purchases.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must exercise reasonable care in designing features like infinite scrolling, autoplay, notifications, and streak rewards so they do not contribute to foreseeable harms to minors, including eating disorders, depression and anxiety tied to compulsive use, harassment, sexual exploitation, drug and gambling exposure, and financial harm [S3].

The most protective privacy and safety settings must be on by default for users a platform knows are minors, including limiting who can contact them, restricting public access to their personal data, dialing back addictive design features, and offering a prominent opt-out of personalized recommendation feeds in favor of a chronological one [S3].

Parents of children under 13 must get parental tools enabled by default, including the ability to view and change privacy settings, restrict purchases, and see and limit total time spent on the platform [S3].

Platforms may not advertise narcotic drugs, cannabis, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to users known to be minors, must provide easy ways to report harm to minors with a substantive response within 10 days for large platforms, and may not run market research on children under 13 at all [S3].

Large platforms must publish annual public reports based on an independent third-party audit, disclosing how many minors use the platform, how much time they spend, and how well safeguards work, and must open their systems and data to those auditors [S3].

Title II requires any platform whose algorithm ranks content using personal data users did not explicitly hand over to notify users and let them easily switch to a version of the feed that does not use that data, and bars platforms from charging users more for making that switch [S3].
Enforcement would run through the Federal Trade Commission under its existing penalty structure, and state attorneys general could sue platforms directly on behalf of their residents [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, social media companies, online video game makers, and streaming services would bear the cost of redesigning engagement-maximizing features, building new controls and reporting systems, and submitting to annual audits. Platform advertising revenue tied to minors' attention could fall as addictive-by-default features are dialed back and algorithmic feeds become optional. Users of all ages would see new notices about algorithmic feeds, and free services might monetize differently to cover compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Social media, gaming, and streaming companies

drawbacks.text: The duty of care reaches subjective categories like depressive disorders, anxiety, and harassment tied to platform use [S3]. Civil liberties groups including the ACLU and EFF warned during the prior Congress that such a standard could pressure platforms to suppress lawful speech about LGBTQ+ identity, mental health, and politics for minors to avoid liability, and the bill's own carve-out bars enforcement based only on First Amendment-protected viewpoints without fully resolving the concern [S3].

Parental tools give parents the ability to view and, for children under 13, control a minor's privacy and account settings [S3]. Advocates for LGBTQ+ youth and domestic-abuse survivors have warned that surveillance-style parental controls can endanger minors in unaccepting or abusive households, and the bill explicitly says it will not mandate age verification, leaving age a largely self-declared matter that platforms may only infer [S3].

Compliance and audit obligations fall on every covered platform regardless of size, though reporting-and-response deadlines are longer for platforms under 10 million monthly US users, and the bill directs a federal study on whether device-level age verification could burden small companies [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections for minors are concrete and the enforcement mechanisms are real: default-on safety settings, a ban on drug and gambling ads to minors, independent audits, and two enforcement paths. The strongest honest objection is that a broadly worded duty of care could tempt platforms to over-block lawful content for minors, and that parental controls can be misused against vulnerable teens. On balance the bill is a serious, if imperfect, attempt to shift the cost of a documented child mental-health problem off families and onto the companies profiting from minors' attention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for 15 months, and on August 5, 2026 the committee voted to report it favorably with an amended substitute text; it now awaits action on the Senate floor and has never been taken up by the House.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 14, 2025 by Sen. Marsha Blackburn with Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer as the other original sponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee [S5].
It drew 76 Senate cosponsors, split 42 Republicans, 33 Democrats, and 1 independent, more than the two-thirds majority needed to override a veto [S4].
On August 5, 2026, the Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, meaning the committee approved a rewritten version [S5].
The Senate has not yet voted on the bill, and the House has taken no recorded action on it in this Congress [S1].
An earlier version of this same bill, S. 1409 in the 118th Congress, passed the Senate by unanimous consent in July 2024 but never received a House floor vote before that Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No final winner yet, since the bill is still alive. So far the platforms are ahead on timing: a bill with 76 Senate cosponsors took 15 months to clear a single committee, and the same bill died in the House without a vote last Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support is heavily bipartisan: of 76 cosponsors, 42 are Republicans, 33 are Democrats, and 1 is an independent, and the bill's four original sponsors include the top leaders of both parties [S4].

industries.note: The bill targets engagement-maximizing design — infinite scroll, autoplay, streaks, notification loops — that platforms use to keep minors online and advertising to them. Default-on safety settings, an opt-out of algorithmic feeds, annual third-party audits of minor usage, and state AG enforcement would cut directly into that business model, so platforms' commercial interest runs against the minors and parents the bill serves.

The bill covers online games, defines microtransactions including loot-box-style surprise mechanics, requires safeguards against compulsive usage, and requires parent-viewable metrics and purchase restrictions. It is softened for games — safeguards need not interrupt gameplay, and purchases with in-game currency earned purely through play are excluded.

Covered services get a lighter compliance path if their content is provider-selected rather than user-generated, needing only parental controls, limits on autoplay, and no ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol aimed at minors. The general burden still applies where they run recommendation-driven feeds for minors.

The bill does not mandate age gating, but it orders a federal study of device-level age verification and lets platforms contract with third parties to provide the required safeguards, creating a potential market for compliance vendors.

analysis.trajectory: With a favorable committee report in hand and 76 cosponsors including both Senate leaders, a Senate floor vote is plausible this session. The bigger hurdle is the House, which took no action on the nearly identical S. 1409 after the Senate passed it unanimously in 2024; without House leadership scheduling a vote, the bill could again pass or clear the Senate only to stall. The committee substitute text may also draw new objections from civil liberties and tech groups that could slow a floor deal.
